title: Bouncing ball

reference.basis: banded black-and-white stick with ten segments is a standard 1 m metre stick

slow_motion.evidence: no caption, text or visual indication of slow motion; motion looks like real-time animation

subjects.description: small orange cartoon ball with white highlight

observation.what_happens: An orange ball drops from the upper left, hits the brown floor and bounces repeatedly while drifting to the right. It is still bouncing toward the lower right when the clip ends, never being caught or stopping.

calibration.note: black-and-white striped bar = 1 m (banded black-and-white stick with ten segments is a standard 1 m metre stick) spans 351 px in SAM's mask

given: scale: black-and-white striped bar = 1 m (banded black-and-white stick with ten segments is a standard 1 m metre stick) spans 351 px in SAM's mask, known to ±30%
reasoning: x drifts steadily right while y shows repeated parabolic-like arcs hitting near -0.74 m, so all models need gravity plus a restitution bounce event. Fall is very slow for 0.7 m, implying large air effect or small effective g, so we compete vacuum vs linear vs quadratic drag with floor loss.

law.title: Bouncing ball in vacuum
law.summary: Gravity only and a bouncy floor that keeps some up-down speed each hit.

fitted.title: Bouncing ball in vacuum
fitted.summary: Gravity only and a bouncy floor that keeps some up-down speed each hit.

candidates.ifItWins: Flight is ballistic with constant horizontal speed and bounce height ratio set only by restitution.

law.title: Bouncing ball with linear air drag
law.summary: Gravity plus air resistance that grows with speed and a bouncy floor.

fitted.title: Bouncing ball with linear air drag
fitted.summary: Gravity plus air resistance that grows with speed and a bouncy floor.

candidates.ifItWins: Air slows the light ball proportional to velocity, rounding the arcs and limiting fall speed.

law.title: Bouncing ball with quadratic air drag
law.summary: Gravity plus speed-squared air drag and a bounce that loses up-down and sideways speed.

params.name: fx
params.meaning: tangential retention vx after = fx*vx before

fitted.title: Bouncing ball with quadratic air drag
fitted.summary: Gravity plus speed-squared air drag and a bounce that loses up-down and sideways speed.

params.name: fx
params.meaning: tangential retention vx after = fx*vx before

candidates.ifItWins: Fast motion feels air drag as speed squared and the bounce scrubs some sideways speed.

law.title: Textbook projectile (no air)
law.summary: Moves at constant horizontal speed while gravity pulls it down at a constant rate.

fitted.title: Textbook projectile (no air)
fitted.summary: Moves at constant horizontal speed while gravity pulls it down at a constant rate.

caveats: Absolute scale from the metre stick is uncertain to about a third, so gravity and floor height in metres share that uncertainty.
Restitution is assumed the same at every bounce and horizontal speed is assumed constant.
critique.finding: The ball falls pulled by gravity of {g} and bounces off a floor at {floor_y}. Each bounce keeps {e} of its upward speed, with no air slowing it.
critique.headline: Bouncing ball falls freely, keeps most bounce energy.
critique.why_it_won: The winner realizes the air does nothing, while the drag model chases slowing that never appears.

headline: Bouncing ball falls freely, keeps most bounce energy.
finding: The ball falls pulled by gravity of 1.01 ± 0.3 m/s² and bounces off a floor at -0.794 ± 0.24 m. Each bounce keeps 0.85 ± 0.0002 of its upward speed, with no air slowing it. That is 9.7× weaker than Earth’s gravity, so the clip most likely plays about 3.1× slower than real life.

eyeball.law_in_words: Ball is a projectile in uniform gravity: horizontal velocity constant, vertical motion free-fall with acceleration -g, bouncing on horizontal floor at y=floor_y with vy_after = -e*vy_before and vx unchanged.

clock.note: Gravity came out 9.7× too weak. Either this happened somewhere with 0.1× Earth’s gravity, or the clip plays about 3.1× slower than real life (slow motion). Run it again with the slow-motion factor set.
